songwriter: Vinícius de Moraes (Portuguese lyrics); Norman Gimbel (later English lyrics)
research_notes: Music by Jobim, Portuguese lyrics by Vinícius de Moraes, 1962. Originally titled 'Menina que Passa' for the unfinished musical comedy Dirigível. First commercial recording 1962 by Pery Ribeiro. English lyrics by Norman Gimbel the following year. Stan Getz / João Gilberto / Astrud Gilberto recording (Getz/Gilberto, recorded March 1963, released March 1964) is the internationally famous version. Year 1962 is the composition and first commercial recording year.

songwriter: Ary Barroso; Bob Russell (later English lyrics)
research_notes: Written by Ary Barroso in 1939 (originally 'Aquarela brasileira'). First recording: Francisco Alves, 18 August 1939, arranged by Radamés Gnattali and his orchestra, Odeon. Performed before recording by Cândido Botelho at the benefit show Joujoux e Balangandans. Year 1939 is both composition and first recording year.

songwriter: Pascual Contursi | Enrique Pedro Maroni (later popular lyrics); Matos Rodríguez also wrote lyrics
research_notes: Composed 1916 in Montevideo by architecture student Gerardo Matos Rodríguez as a march; first performed publicly at Café La Giralda. Orchestra leader Roberto Firpo adapted it as a tango, adding a third section from his own tangos and a fragment of Verdi's Miserere. Firpo recorded it November 1916 for Odeon (release 483) in Buenos Aires. Country of origin is Uruguay; the tango's later life is shared with Argentina. The better-known lyrics are by Argentines Contursi and Maroni.

original_instruments: bandoneón | piano | violin | electric guitar | double bass
research_notes: Composed October 1959 in New York after Piazzolla learned of the death of his father Vicente 'Nonino' Piazzolla. Based on his 1954 Paris tango 'Nonino'. Italian Wikipedia notes a first quintet recording in Montevideo in 1960 (Piazzolla, Jaime Gosis, Quicho Díaz, Horacio Malvicino, Simón Bajour). Year 1959 is the composition year.

Composed 1956 (pt.wikipedia). First recording April 1958 by Elizeth Cardoso on Canção do Amor Demais (Festa), with Jobim arrangements and (uncredited on the original issue) João Gilberto guitar. Gilberto's own version recorded 10 July 1958, released as an EMI-Odeon 78 in August 1958 (B-side 'Bim Bom'), is treated as the start of bossa nova. Reference artist is Gilberto; Cardoso's earlier recording is noted. Year 1958 is the first-release year.

Written and composed by Violeta Parra in La Paz, Bolivia, in 1966; recorded 1966 and included on Las últimas composiciones (RCA Victor), her last album before her death in 1967. Year 1966 is both composition and recording year.

songwriter: Julio Baudouin (as Julio de La Paz) (zarzuela libretto)
research_notes: Composed 1913 by Daniel Alomía Robles for the Peruvian zarzuela El cóndor pasa (libretto Julio Baudouin / Julio de La Paz); first public performance at Teatro Mazzi, Lima. Based on traditional Andean music. Piano arrangement registered 3 May 1933 (Edward B. Marks, Library of Congress no. 9643). Declared Peruvian national cultural heritage 16 March 2004. Simon & Garfunkel's 1970 English version is a later cover. Year 1913 is the composition/premiere year.

Recorded by João Gilberto on 10 November 1958 and released as an Odeon 78 rpm single in February 1959; also on the album Chega de Saudade (March 1959). Music by Antônio Carlos Jobim with Newton Mendonça. Year is the single release year. The Instituto Antônio Carlos Jobim catalogue dates the track 1959.

English Wikipedia and the Instituto Antônio Carlos Jobim catalogue state that João Gilberto first recorded the song in 1960 on O Amor, o Sorriso e a Flor, with music by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Portuguese lyrics by Newton Mendonça. English lyrics by Jon Hendricks came later. Year is that first recording year.

Antônio Carlos Jobim wrote the Portuguese lyric and the English lyric Waters of March in 1972. The first recording was on the 1972 insert EP O Tom de Antonio Carlos Jobim e o Tal de João Bosco. Elis Regina recorded it the same year on the album Elis. The duet with Jobim opens the 1974 album Elis & Tom. Year is the composition and first-release year. The artist field names the duet most often cited as the reference recording.

original_instruments: Piano | Guitar | Double bass | Drums | Flute | Trombone | Strings
research_notes: Title track of Jobim's A&M album Wave, recorded 22–24 May and 15 June 1967 at Van Gelder Studio and released in October 1967. All tracks on the album are credited to Jobim. Personnel lists Jobim on piano, guitar, harpsichord and vocals, so a piano part is documented on the original recording. Arranger Claus Ogerman. Jazzdisco.org lists the same session.

original_instruments: Piano | Guitar | Double bass | Drums | Flute | Strings
research_notes: Track on the 1967 album Wave, credited to Antônio Carlos Jobim, who plays piano on the session. Year is the album release year documented by English Wikipedia and Jazzdisco. Those pages do not state an earlier composition date for this title.

Daniel Thompson's Ary Barroso discography lists Na Baixa do Sapateiro as a samba-jongo by Ary Barroso, performed by Barroso at the piano with Laurindo de Almeida and Garoto on guitars, Odeon 11746-A, recorded 26 June 1939 and released in August 1939. The second source consulted confirms Barroso as a 1939 samba composer but does not discuss this title, so the record stays Partially verified. Piano is the lead instrument on the cited recording.

The same 1939–1941 Barroso discography lists Camisa Amarela as a samba by Ary Barroso, sung by Aracy de Almeida with Conjunto Regional RCA Victor, Victor 34445-A, recorded 31 March 1939 and released in June 1939. No second page consulted discusses this title specifically.

Portuguese Wikipedia says Pixinguinha composed the piece between 1916 and 1917 and that the first recording, instrumental, was in 1928. João de Barro wrote the lyric, and Orlando Silva recorded the sung version in 1937. The Itaú Cultural encyclopaedia also places an instrumental recording in 1928. The composition year is a range given by Pixinguinha, so year here is the 1937 vocal recording. A UNIRIO paper quotes Pixinguinha calling the original a slow polca.

The official Pixinguinha site says the choro was first recorded in 1928 by Orquestra Típica Pixinguinha-Donga on Parlophon 12.867-A under the singular title Lamento, while Pixinguinha's manuscripts use the plural Lamentos. Vinícius de Moraes wrote a lyric in the 1960s; his site credits the sung version to Vinícius de Moraes and Pixinguinha. Year is the 1928 instrumental recording. The 1928 release is instrumental, so language is Instrumental for that recording.

Baião by Luiz Gonzaga and Humberto Teixeira. Portuguese Wikipedia and Discografia Brasileira agree on a 3 March 1947 RCA Victor session and a May 1947 release, with Luiz Gonzaga as the singer. The song describes drought in the Northeast. Forró dancers treat it as a northeastern anthem; the genre on the sources is baião.

Xote by Luiz Gonzaga and Zé Dantas. Portuguese Wikipedia says Gonzaga recorded it on 5 February 1953 for RCA Victor, released in May 1953. The Luiz Gonzaga site lists the same partnership and the 78 rpm issue V801108a (1953).

Opening track of Caetano Veloso's solo album, released January 1968 on Philips, produced by Rogério Duprat according to the song page. The title was suggested by Luiz Carlos Barreto after Hélio Oiticica's installation and later named the Tropicália movement. Composed by Caetano Veloso.

Presented by Caetano Veloso with the Beat Boys at the III Festival de Música Popular Brasileira (TV Record), whose final was on 21 October 1967. The song placed fourth. A Philips single with Remelexo on the B-side was issued in 1967. Sources describe electric guitars as the point of controversy.

Track on Caetano Veloso's January 1968 Philips album. Both the Portuguese and English album pages credit the song to Gilberto Gil and José Carlos Capinam, not to Veloso. Sung in Spanish. Year is the album release year.

Title song of Chico Buarque's Philips album Construção, released in 1971 and produced by Roberto Menescal. The Portuguese album page dates the LP to November 1971 and credits the title track to Chico Buarque. The Instituto site lists the same 1971 Philips album. Arrangements by Magro and Rogério Duprat.

Chico Buarque's song shared first place at the II Festival de Música Popular Brasileira. The final was on 10 October 1966 at Teatro Record Consolação in São Paulo. He sang it with Nara Leão. It tied with Disparada after Buarque refused to take the prize alone. A 22 October 1966 magazine item in the Jobim/Chico archive reports the song's success at that festival. Year is 1966.

The 1967 TV Record festival page lists Roda Viva by Chico Buarque among the notable songs premiered there, with the final on 21 October 1967. História da MPB places it third, sung by Chico Buarque and MPB-4. Year is the festival year.

Written by José Augusto and Paulo Sérgio Valle in 1989. Chitãozinho & Xororó recorded it in October 1990 for the album Cowboy do Asfalto, released 4 December 1990 on PolyGram. English Wikipedia says Leonardo Sullivan had recorded it in 1989 on Veneno, Mel e Sabor without national success. Year is the duo's release year. The duo did not write the song.

songwriter: Antônio Dyggs | Karine Vinagre | Amanda Cruz | Aline Medeiros
original_format: Live vocal recording issued as a single
research_notes: Michel Teló's version was released on 25 July 2011. Portuguese Wikipedia credits Antônio Dyggs, Sharon Acioly, Karine Vinagre, Amanda Cruz and Aline Medeiros after a 2012 authorship settlement reported by Rolling Stone Brasil. Further co-authorship claims by other students were still in court in the pages consulted. The song is filed as sertanejo because that is the style of Teló's hit version; English Wikipedia also describes it as pop.

Gilberto Gil and Os Mutantes placed second with this song at the III Festival da Record; the final was 21 October 1967. Arranger Rogério Duprat. A single is dated November 1967 on the 1968 album page, which also includes the track. Rolling Stone Brasil confirms the second-place festival result and the 1968 album. Year is the festival year.

Samba by Gilberto Gil, recorded April–May 1969 and released in August 1969 on Philips, before his exile in London. Itaú Cultural says it was first sung in public on 20–21 July 1969 at Teatro Castro Alves in the show Barra 69. The lyric names Rio neighbourhoods, samba schools and Realengo, where Gil had been held.

Opening track of Gilberto Gil's 1969 Philips album, recorded April–May 1969. The album page lists no other composer for this track, while it names other writers where the song is not Gil's. The Aquele Abraço page confirms the same album and session window. A separate song article was not consulted.

Written by Gilberto Gil and Caetano Veloso and recorded by Os Mutantes in 1968. It opens their June 1968 Polydor debut and also appears on Tropicália ou Panis et Circencis. A Discogs copy of the collective album prints the recording period as May 1968. Rita Lee, Arnaldo Baptista and Sérgio Dias sing it, with an arrangement by Rogério Duprat. Spellings Circencis and Circenses both appear on the records.
Second track of Os Mutantes' June 1968 debut. The album page credits the song to Jorge Ben. The group did not write it. Year is the album release year.

Track on Os Mutantes (Polydor, June 1968). The album page credits Maria Fulô to Humberto Teixeira and Sivuca. The page classifies the album as Tropicália and psychedelic rock and does not give a separate genre label for this track. Year is the album release.

Written and sung by Jorge Ben. English Wikipedia dates the Philips single and the album Samba Esquema Novo to 10 January 1963. Discografia Brasileira says the Philips 78 rpm (Mas que nada / Por causa de você, menina), with Copa 5, came out in July 1963 and the LP about two months later. Both agree on 1963, Jorge Ben and Philips. The YouTube link returned in search is a Universal Music Group upload of the album track. Sérgio Mendes's 1966 cover is better known outside Brazil.

Jorge Ben wrote the song. Wilson Simonal recorded the first released version on 22 July 1969; Odeon issued it in August 1969. Ben's own version is on the Philips album Jorge Ben, released November 1969 according to the English album page and December 1969 according to the Portuguese song page. The artist field is Simonal because the sources identify his recording as the first. Later the song was more often associated with Ben.

Samba by Adoniran Barbosa, released in 1964 and made famous by Demônios da Garoa. IMMuB lists the Chantecler LP Trem das Onze (CMG 2294, 1964) by Demônios da Garoa with this title as track 1, credited to Adoniran Barbosa. The lyric refers to the Tramway da Cantareira and the Jaçanã neighbourhood of São Paulo.

Zequinha de Abreu's choro was first played in 1917 in Santa Rita do Passa Quatro under the title Tico-Tico no Farelo. It was renamed in 1931 and first recorded that year by Orquestra Colbaz (Columbia). IMSLP lists the composition year as 1917 and includes piano arrangements, so a published piano version is documented. Year is the composition year. The 1917 piece was instrumental; lyrics by Aloysio de Oliveira and others came later.

Samba by Cartola. The song page says Beth Carvalho's 1976 album Mundo Melhor was the first commercial release, and that Cartola's own voice-and-guitar version is on his second Discos Marcus Pereira album the same year. Discogs dates that album to 1976 and lists the track. The song page's infobox also shows 1974; the body text and the album page support 1976, which is the year used here.

Opening samba on Cartola's second album, Discos Marcus Pereira, 1976. The album page says the recording is accompanied by Guinga on guitar. Discogs lists O Mundo É um Moinho on the 1976 album Cartola. Composer credit on that page is Cartola.
Included on Cartola's 1976 Discos Marcus Pereira album. The album article names it with As Rosas não Falam and O Mundo É um Moinho. Discogs lists Preciso Me Encontrar on the 1976 master.

Tied for first place with A Banda at the II Festival de MPB; the final was 10 October 1966. The festival table credits the song to Geraldo Vandré and the performance to Jair Rodrigues. The A Banda article adds Théo de Barros as co-author and names Trio Marayá and Trio Novo as additional performers. História da MPB calls it a toada. The split of music and lyrics between Vandré and de Barros is not stated on the pages consulted, so both names are in the songwriter and composer fields as co-authors.

Won the III Festival de Música Popular Brasileira. The final was 21 October 1967. Edu Lobo and Marília Medalha sang it, with Momento Quatro. Authors on the festival page and on História da MPB are Edu Lobo and Capinam. The page does not separate music and lyrics.

The 1966 festival final table lists Ensaio Geral by Gilberto Gil, sung by Elis Regina, in fifth place. The final was 10 October 1966. A second page consulted mentions the festival date but not this title, so the song credit rests on the festival article.

Third place at the 10 October 1966 festival final. The table credits Canção para Maria to Paulinho da Viola and Capinam and the performance to Jair Rodrigues. Music and lyrics are not separated on that page.
Second place at the II Festival de MPB final on 10 October 1966, sung by Elza Soares. The festival table names Adualto Santos Panamá as the author. No second source consulted discusses this title.

Performed by Leny Eversong at the 10 October 1966 festival final. The table credits Carlos Lira and G. Guarnieri. Carlos Lira is the spelling on that page for the composer usually indexed as Carlos Lyra. The record uses the name as printed and does not place the song among the prizewinners.

Sung by Roberto Carlos at the 10 October 1966 festival final. The table credits Célio Borges Pereira. The song was not among the placed winners on that table. No second source consulted discusses the title.

The 1966 festival final table lists Um Dia by Caetano Veloso, sung by Maria Odete (also spelled Maria Odette on the same page's related text). The final was 10 October 1966. The song was not a prizewinner on that table.
Sung by Nara Leão at the 10 October 1966 festival final. The table credits Millôr Fernandes. Not listed among the prizewinners.
Fourth place at the 10 October 1966 festival final, performed by MPB4. The table credits Sérgio Bittencourt. No second source consulted discusses this title.

The 1967 festival page lists Ventania by Geraldo Vandré and Hilton Acioli, sung by Vandré, as a finalist in the third eliminatory on 14 October 1967. História da MPB's festival note does not itemise this title, so the credit rests mainly on the festival article.

Marcha nº 1 of Clube Carnavalesco Misto Vassourinhas, the best-known frevo of the Recife–Olinda carnival. Portuguese Wikipedia, citing a 1949 declaration by Joana Batista Ramos, dates the piece to 6 January 1909 and names her and Mathias da Rocha. A February 2026 Folha de S.Paulo report says documents show Mathias Theodoro da Rocha died in July 1907, which conflicts with a 1909 composition date and with a 1910 sale receipt. First commercial recording cited on Wikipedia: Continental, 1945, Déo and Castro Barbosa. Year is left empty because the composition date is disputed. Artist is Traditional because no single undisputed author is settled in the sources.

title_english: The Day That You Love Me
research_notes: Tango with music by Carlos Gardel and lyrics by Alfredo Le Pera, written for the 1935 Paramount film of the same name. The Spanish article's body says the first recording was in New York on 19 March 1935 for RCA Victor; its infobox prints 1934. The English film page places the song in the 1935 film. Year 1935 follows the article body and the film page. The film was made in the United States; the tango is filed under Argentina as Gardel's repertoire.

Spanish Wikipedia says Gardel composed it with a lyric by Alfredo Le Pera for the film Tango Bar (1935), and dates publication to 19 March 1935. The Spanish Wikipedia tango article also names it among Gardel and Le Pera's tangos. The title is Rioplatense racing slang for winning by a head. Both pages are Wikipedia, so the record stays Partially verified.

The Spanish Wikipedia tango article says Gardel sang Mi noche triste in 1917, music by Samuel Castriota and lyric by Pascual Contursi, and treats that performance as the start of tango-canción. The lyric incipit quoted there is Percanta que me amuraste. A second page consulted in this batch does not independently document the 1917 date, so the record is Partially verified.

original_instruments: Bandoneon | Piano | Electric bass | Drums | Guitar | Flute | Strings
research_notes: Instrumental by Astor Piazzolla, recorded in May 1974 at Mondial Sound in Milan and released in 1974 on Carosello. English and Spanish Wikipedia and the Discogs master agree on Piazzolla as the author, 1974, and the tango nuevo framing. The title joins libertad and tango. Pino Presti is credited with the electric bass line. Piazzolla's country of musical association is Argentina; the session was in Italy.

Tango written entirely by Enrique Santos Discépolo in 1934. Spanish Wikipedia says Sofía Bozán premiered it at the end of 1934 at Teatro Maipo in Buenos Aires, at Discépolo's request. In the 1935 film El alma del bandoneón it was sung by Ernesto Famá with Francisco Lomuto's orchestra. The Discépolo article's tango table also dates it to 1934.

Lyric and music by Enrique Santos Discépolo. The song article says 1929; the Discépolo article's table says 1930; LetrasTango dates the premiere by Sofía Bozán to 24 August 1930 at Teatro Sarmiento and the first dated recording, Orquesta Típica Victor with Alberto Gómez and Augusto Vila, to 4 September 1930. Carlos Gardel recorded it on 16 October 1930. Year 1930 is the premiere and first recording year used by LetrasTango. The 1929 date remains in Wikipedia.

The Discépolo article's selected-tango table dates Uno to 1943, with lyric by Enrique Santos Discépolo and music by Mariano Mores. The tango overview article names Uno among Discépolo's songs but does not repeat the year or the Mores credit. No first performer is named on the pages consulted, so the artist field uses Discépolo as the credited author most closely tied to the work.

The Discépolo discography table lists Malevaje in 1929 with lyric by Discépolo and music by Juan de Dios Filiberto. The tango article names the song among Discépolo's works and does not repeat the Filiberto credit. First singer is not stated on the pages consulted.

Spanish Wikipedia says the tango was premiered in 1903 by José Luis Roncallo's orchestra at the restaurant El Americano in Buenos Aires and that the score was published in 1905, under Villoldo's name. It also says the melody is sometimes attributed to Casimiro Alcorta and may date from about 1898. IMSLP lists a piano setting and gives a first performance of 1903. English Wikipedia dates publication to 1903 and the premiere to El Americano. The original Villoldo text was about corn; the best-known lyric is a later one by Discépolo (1947), not the original. Year 1903 is the premiere year. Authorship is not unanimous, so the record is Partially verified.

Lyric by Homero Manzi, music by Lucio Demare, written in 1941. Premiered by Demare's orchestra with Juan Carlos Miranda at the Novelty. The recording that made it famous is Aníbal Troilo with Francisco Fiorentino, RCA Victor, 8 January 1942. tango.info dates the work 1942 and credits Demare and Manzi. The film El viejo Hucha, directed by Lucas Demare, premiered on 29 April 1942. Year is the first famous recording year. Artist is Troilo's orchestra, with Fiorentino as the singer named in the sources.

Instrumental tango by Osvaldo Pugliese, 1946. MusicBrainz and a 78 rpm archive page date the first recording to 21 August 1946 in Buenos Aires, Odeon, matrix 15758. English Wikipedia calls it Pugliese's signature rhythmic tango. The title is an onomatopoeia for the bandoneon attack. Bibletango gives the composition date as 1943, which is not followed here because the recording sources and Wikipedia use 1946.

Zamba by the Mendoza businessman Luis Hermenegildo Profili, registered at SADAIC on 24 April 1964 under the pseudonym Luis H. Morales and the title De mi esperanza. Jorge Cafrune's recording on Emoción, canto y guitarra (CBS, 1964) spread it. Los Chalchaleros recorded it in 1965 as De mi esperanza. Listeners renamed it from the first line. Profili was from San Martín, Mendoza, not from the Northwest.

León Gieco wrote it in 1978 in Cañada Rosquín, Santa Fe. The Spanish song page and the album page 4.º L.P. say the album was released in 1979; English Wikipedia calls 4to. LP a 1978 album. The album page describes a studio take with bandoneonist Dino Saluzzi during the 1978 sessions. Year 1978 is the composition year. Radio Nacional has a page dated 26 July 1979 about registration of the song; that page was seen in search but is a short notice.

Edmundo P. Zaldívar, a Buenos Aires guitarist, composed this carnavalito in 1941 on the way to Radio El Mundo, before he had visited the Northwest. La Nación reports a 1943 piano-sheet cover that calls it a carnavalito and danza típica indo criolla. The Universidad Nacional del Litoral catalogue lists a piano score, Buenos Aires, Tierra Linda, about 1943. A Jujuy decree of 30 September 1954 declared it regional music and dance of the province. Year is the composition year given in the biography and in La Nación.

Los Chalchaleros, formed in Salta, debuted on 16 June 1948 at Teatro Alberdi. The group article says the first song they sang in public was Zamba del grillo by Atahualpa Yupanqui. The composition year of Yupanqui's zamba is not given on the pages consulted. Year is the debut performance year. A second page was used only to confirm the group's later folklore role, not this title.

Included on Las últimas composiciones (RCA Victor, November 1966). Spanish Wikipedia says the song was composed in 1962 and released on that 1966 album. Year is the release year. English Wikipedia also treats it as Parra's song from that album.

Violeta Parra's Spanish Wikipedia biography says the 1959 Odeon albums La tonada and La cueca include her setting of her brother Nicanor Parra's poem Cueca larga de los Meneses. A second page consulted confirms her as a nueva canción composer but does not discuss this title. Year is the album year given in the biography.

Spanish Wikipedia says Víctor Jara composed the song in 1969. It is on the album Pongo en tus manos abiertas... and is the B-side of the 1969 Jota Jota single whose A-side is Plegaria a un labrador. On that single the B-side is sung by Jara alone. The names Amanda and Manuel in the lyric are his parents' names, according to the song article.

title_original: El derecho de vivir en paz
title_english: The Right to Live in Peace
research_notes: Title song of Víctor Jara's sixth solo album, DICAP, April 1971. The Fundación Víctor Jara lists it as track 1 of the original edition. The song article says it was written in 1969 as a protest against the Vietnam War. The album page says most songs are by Jara and names Plegaria a un labrador, not this title, as the piece composed with Patricio Castillo. Electric guitars and organ come from the collaboration with Los Blops. Year is the album release year.

A-side of the 1969 Jota Jota single JJS-101, sung by Víctor Jara with Quilapayún. The single page credits Víctor Jara and Patricio Castillo. The 1971 album article says Plegaria a un labrador was composed together with Patricio Castillo, and the Fundación track list includes it on side B of the 1971 LP. Year is the single year.

title_original: El pueblo unido jamás será vencido
title_english: The People United Will Never Be Defeated
research_notes: Music by Sergio Ortega; the text is credited to Sergio Ortega and Quilapayún. Quilapayún's official song page and press page document a 1973 premiere, but they do not agree on the day: one account says 21 June 1973 and another places a debut on the Alameda in August 1973. An academic paper by Karmy and Farías places the composition in mid-1973 in Santiago. The studio recording is dated 1974 on the official site. Year is 1973 for the composition and public premiere, not the studio date.

title_original: El baile de los que sobran
title_english: The Dance of Those Left Over
original_instruments: Voice | Electric guitar | Drum machine | Synthesizer
research_notes: Written by Jorge González for Los Prisioneros' album Pateando piedras (EMI Odeón Chilena, 1986). Memoria Chilena, the National Library of Chile, and both Wikipedia language editions date the song to 1986 and credit González. He has described writing it with a small drum machine and a Casio keyboard, with acoustic guitar by Claudio Narea added later.

Paseo vallenato by Emiliano Zuleta Baquero, 1938, from a piqueria with Lorenzo Morales (Moralito). Spanish and English Wikipedia and a La Tercera article agree on Zuleta and 1938. Guillermo Buitrago later recorded a version as Que Criterio and claimed authorship. Carlos Vives's 1990s recording made it an international hit; that version is a later cover, not the original record.

Juan Madera Castro wrote the instrumental cumbia in 1960 while playing clarinet in Pedro Salcedo's orchestra; Wilson Choperena added the lyric months later. Spanish Wikipedia says the definitive version is the Discos Tropical 78 rpm recorded in Barranquilla in 1961, with Choperena singing and Madera on clarinet. The work was notarised on 24 October 1962. English Wikipedia has given a later date for the lyric. Year is the 1961 Tropical recording. A 2010 court ruling treated Madera and Choperena as co-authors, with Madera as composer.

Salsa by Joe Arroyo, recorded with La Verdad on the album Musa Original (Discos Fuentes, 1986). English Wikipedia dates the song to 1986 and notes its relation to his earlier piece El Mulato (1978). The artist site lists the album and the track. The site's editorial dates are from 2026 and are not used as the song's year. Also known by the subtitle No le pegue a la negra.

Cumbia by José Benito Barros. Semana and Radio Enciclopedia say he finished it in the late 1960s and that the first recording was by Trío Los Inseparables in 1969. English Wikipedia identifies the song and the composer and does not give a year. Year is the first-recording year from the magazine and radio accounts.

Cumbia by Lucho Bermúdez, from his 1970 CBS album of the same name, with vocals by Matilde Díaz. English and Spanish Wikipedia agree on the composer, the year and the singer. Later use in the film Encanto is a reuse of a 1970 popular song, not the song's origin.

Vals by María Isabel Granda Larco (Chabuca Granda). Spanish Wikipedia and the Peruvian Ministry of Culture agree that she signed it on 7 January 1950 and that it was premiered on 21 July 1950. The first recording cited on the Spanish page is Los Morochucos in 1953. English Wikipedia gives a conflicting 1950 recording date for Los Morochucos. Year is the 1950 composition and premiere.

Vals by Felipe Pinglo Alva. Spanish Wikipedia places the composition in the early 1930s, a possible premiere in 1931 by Alcides Carreño and Pedro Espinel at Teatro Alfonso XIII in Callao, publication of the lyric in El Cancionero de Lima in 1934, and the first disc by Los Trovadores del Perú in 1943 (Odeón, Buenos Aires). The melody was later confused with the Argentine waltz Mi Marta. Year is left empty because the sources do not settle a single composition year.

Afro-Peruvian song from San Luis de Cañete. Spanish Wikipedia says Perú Negro staged Caitro Soto's version in the early 1970s and published it on the 1973 album Gran Premio del Festival Hispanoamericano de la Danza y la Canción. Celia Cruz recorded a salsa version in 1974. No composition year is stated. Year is the 1973 album. The melody is treated as traditional, with Soto as the arranger of the version Perú Negro used.

Huayno from Cusco. The melody was written in 1942 by Miguel Ángel Hurtado Delgado as Tusuy; his brother Evencio wrote the Quechua lyric, and the song was entered in a 1945 Cusco folklore contest under the name Valicha, for Valeriana Huillca. Instituto Raíces and RPP tell that sequence. Spanish Wikipedia's publication year and English Wikipedia's 1945 writing date do not match. Year 1945 is the contest year of the known Quechua song.

Joropo from the zarzuela Alma llanera. Music by Pedro Elías Gutiérrez, lyric by Rafael Bolívar Coronado. Premiered on 19 September 1914 at Teatro Caracas. The Banda Marcial de Caracas played it in public on 31 December 1914 at Plaza Bolívar. First printed in 1915. The Venezuelan culture ministry and the National Library document the centenary of that premiere. Sources say it draws on the joropo Marisela and the waltz Mita. Filed here as Venezuelan joropo repertoire; the zarzuela origin is noted.

Pasaje by Simón Díaz, not a joropo. Track B1 of the 1980 album Golpe y Pasaje (Palacio LPS-66479). Recorded at Audio Uno in Caracas with the Conjunto Criollo de Cándido Herrera. Spanish and English Wikipedia and the Sincopa LP note agree on Díaz, the title and 1980. Later use of verses by the Gipsy Kings is a separate adaptation.

English Wikipedia says the joropo was written in 1958 and first recorded that year by Mario Suárez for Kubaney, and that Hugo Blanco's 1961 recording was the hit. Spanish Wikipedia credits only José Manzo Perroni. MusicBrainz has listed both Manzo Perroni and Hugo Blanco. The composer field is left empty because the sources do not agree. Year 1958 is the first recording year given by English Wikipedia.

The Zitarrosa discography annex lists a 1968 Orfeo single (90003) with Doña Soledad on side A and the 1968 album Yo sé quién soy (Orfeo ULP 90504) with the song as track 2. A Radio Educación interview says he composed this candombe in 1969 while speaking from exile, which conflicts with the 1968 release. Year is the release year on the discography. Genre is taken from the interview, which calls it a candombe.

Opens the 1965 Tonal EP El canto de Zitarrosa (CP 5017). The discography annex lists it again on later Orfeo issues. The artist biography page identifies Zitarrosa but does not discuss this title, so the track credit rests on the discography. Genre follows the word milonga in the title and the EP's place in his early folk-song catalogue. A separate composer credit is not printed on the table.

Track on side B of the 1966 Tonal album Canta Zitarrosa (CP 040), repeated on the 1969 Orfeo issue of that album. The discography does not name a composer. Genre is taken from the title. Year is the first album year on the annex.

Guarania by José Asunción Flores. The lyric long associated with it is by Manuel Ortiz Guerrero; an earlier lyric by Rigoberto Fontao Meza was replaced. Flores and Ortiz Guerrero met in 1928. A decree of 24 July 1944 declared India an official song. No single composition year is stated on the pages consulted. The musicaparaguaya biography dates the creation of the guarania form to 1925 and, in another passage, questions the claim that Jejuí was the first work.

Named among Flores's early guaranias. English Wikipedia's guarania article calls Jejuí the first guarania. The musicaparaguaya.org.py biography says Flores created the guarania in 1925 and also prints a score caption that rejects the claim that Jejuí was his first work. Year is empty because of that conflict. The title is Guaraní.

Listed with the guaranias Flores wrote with Manuel Ortiz Guerrero after they met in 1928. The Spanish article glosses the title as Mariposa brillante. English Wikipedia's guarania overview names Panambí Vera among the best-known guaranias and does not give a year. Year is empty.

Music by Demetrio Ortiz, written in 1948 in Córdoba according to the Spanish article and Asunción City. Lyrics by Zulema de Mirkin, associated with a 1950 meeting in ABC Color's account. First performance cited as 1951. Year is the music year. The lyric is in Spanish and uses the Guaraní word kuñataĩ.

Asunción City says Demetrio Ortiz composed this guarania in 1943 in Concepción and dedicated it to his mother. The Folkways Harps of Paraguay booklet credits María Teresa Márquez and Demetrio Ortiz and does not give a year. English Wikipedia's guarania article names the song and does not date it. Year 1943 rests on Asunción City.

Paraguayan polca on Smithsonian Folkways SFW CD 40548, Harps of Paraguay (2009). The booklet says Pérez Cardozo used it to open his shows in Argentina. No composition year is printed. The 2009 date is the Folkways album, not the piece.

Paraguayan polca on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The booklet says Santiago Cortesi dedicated it to his hometown, Isla Saká in Caazapá. No composition year is given. Recorded there by Marcelo Rojas, harp, with guitar and bass.
Credited to Lorenzo Leguizamón on the Folkways SFW CD 40548 track list and described in the notes as a Paraguayan polca. No composition year is given.
Credited to Julián Alarcón on the Folkways SFW CD 40548 track list. The booklet classifies the album's harp pieces as Paraguayan polcas. No composition year is given.

Paraguayan polca by Félix Pérez Cardozo on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The notes say the harp imitates a bell, a train whistle and locomotive wheels, and that the piece refers to the train that brought milk into Asunción. No composition year is given.

Paraguayan polca by Herminio Giménez on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The booklet says he first conceived it for an orquesta típica and that the title joins Guaraní jeroky (dance) and popó (vivacious). No composition year is given.

Folkways SFW CD 40548 calls Pájaro campana anonymous and credits Félix Pérez Cardozo's harp arrangement. ABC Color and Portal Guaraní, citing a 1959 notarial statement, say Ampelio Villalba composed Guyra campana around 1914 and that Pérez Cardozo registered an arrangement of a popular motif. English Wikipedia has called it Pérez Cardozo's own composition; that claim is not followed here. Year is empty.
Credited to Prudencio Giménez on the Folkways SFW CD 40548 track list. No composition year is given. The album notes treat these harp pieces as Paraguayan polcas.
Paraguayan polca on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The booklet says harpist Alejandro Villamayor composed it for the town of Unión in San Pedro Department. No composition year is given.

Paraguayan polca by Digno García on Folkways SFW CD 40548. The notes describe a programmatic harp piece in 6/8 and name it with Pájaro campana and Tren lechero as a frequently played harp solo. No composition year is given.

Paraguayan polca on Folkways SFW CD 40548, credited to Kike Pedersen. The notes say maiteí means greetings in Guaraní and describe Pedersen combining traditional polca with a newer harmonic vocabulary. No composition year is given. The 2009 date is the album.

Folkways SFW CD 40548 calls this polca anonymous and associates it with popular festivities in the town of Paraguarí. No date is given. The booklet says it is often played for dance by a banda folclórica.

The English notes of Folkways SFW CD 40548 say folk harpist José del Rosario Diarte composed this Paraguayan polca. The copyright line printed with the track list credits Félix Pérez Cardozo. The notes are followed for the composer, and the conflicting credit is recorded here. No composition year is given. Carretaguy is explained in the booklet as a Guaraní title for life under the cart.

Recorded by Los Kjarkas in 1981 for Canto a la mujer de mi pueblo and issued as the B-side of a 1982 single. English Wikipedia calls the genre Afro-Bolivian saya and credits Ulises Hermosa and Gonzalo Hermosa. Spanish Wikipedia's infobox has also called it caporales. El País reports the later unauthorised use by Kaoma as Lambada (1989). Year is the 1981 recording.

songwriter: Jorge Carrera Andrade, Jorge Enrique Adoum, Hugo Alemán, Jaime Valencia
research_notes: Danzante written on the night of 7 November 1950 at the house of Oswaldo Guayasamín. Music by Gonzalo Benítez; the lyric is by the poets named in the songwriter field. Spanish Wikipedia, the Universidad Andina Simón Bolívar journal and the Dúo Benítez-Valencia article agree. The duo's recording is dated 1956. Year is the 1950 writing night.

Pasacalle. El Comercio and the Museo del Pasillo say Alfredo Carpio Flores registered the music on 18 January 1947. The lyric is attributed to Luis Alberto Valencia, who recorded it in 1947. Also called Chullita quiteño. The lyric credit is journalistic rather than a registry line, so the record stays Partially verified.

Pasillo by the Quito composer César Guerrero Tamayo. Spanish Wikipedia, the Museo del Pasillo and a 2004 El Universo letter agree on the author. The date is disputed: one account says 1930, and Julio Pazos Barrera has said it was already circulating in 1918. It may have been written while Guerrero lived in Pasto, Colombia. Year is empty. The song is filed under Ecuador, his country.

The anthology Pasillos y pasilleros del Ecuador lists El alma en los labios with lyric by Medardo Ángel Silva and music by Francisco Paredes Herrera. No year is printed in the contents entry consulted. A second page used in this batch documents Ecuadorian pasillo as a genre and does not discuss this title.

The same anthology lists the pasillo El beso as lyric and music by Ramón Moya Alzamora (Quito, 1897–1963) and says he directed La Lira Quiteña, organised in 1925. No composition year for El beso is stated in the passage consulted.
The anthology's contents list Cumandá with lyric by Benjamín Ruiz y Gómez and music by Estanislao Pesantez. No year is given in that entry. Only this contents credit was used.

Dave Martins has written that he composed the song in Guyana in the 1970s at the Pegasus hotel after Pat Cameron of Radio Demerara asked him for a song about the country. Tourism Guyana calls the Tradewinds a Caribbean string band and says the song became an anthem during the Essequibo dispute. BBC Radio 3 lists it as a Guyanese heritage track. No exact year is stated. The song does not name Venezuela.

Dutch Wikipedia says Julius Theodoor Hugo Uiterloo, known as Lieve Hugo, from Paramaribo, performed Langa Bere at the Holland Festival in the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam in 1970. English Wikipedia identifies him as a kaseko singer. The composer of this title is not stated. Year is the documented performance year. Lyric language is not stated on the pages consulted.

Dutch Wikipedia calls Srefidensi his song and says it placed ninth in a 2013 public Srefidensi Top 38 marking 38 years of Surinamese independence. No composition or recording year is given. The 2013 date is the poll, not the song.

Spanish Wikipedia lists Chacarera del rancho among songs Los Hermanos Ábalos, formed in Santiago del Estero in 1939, brought into the Argentine folk repertoire. A performers' note says Adolfo Ábalos registered it at SADAIC in 1968; the same document's layout also shows a 1965 SADAIC line that is hard to assign. A folklore blog places the music in the late 1950s in Mar del Plata and the lyric later. Year is empty because those dates conflict. The group used voices, guitars, piano and bombo legüero.

LetrasTango and Bibletango date the milonga to 1931, music by Sebastián Piana and lyric by Homero Manzi, and say Mercedes Simone premiered it and recorded it for Victor in October 1932. MusicBrainz dates the composer and lyricist credits to 1932. Year 1931 follows the composition date used by LetrasTango. The record is Partially verified because of the 1932 database date.

Composed by Roberto Ternán of Salta in the early 1970s after he met a Uruguayan dancer, José, in the Buceo neighbourhood of Montevideo. Los Tucu Tucu recorded it in 1973. Illapu's Andean arrangement, with quena and charango, is on Despedida del pueblo (1976) and is the version La Tercera and a choral-score note describe as the widely known one. Year is that 1976 recording. The composer is Argentine; the rhythm is Uruguayan candombe. This is not a Rubén Rada song.

Released as a single on 14 August 1992, recorded in July 1992 at WR studio in Salvador, produced by Liminha. Portuguese Wikipedia says Tote Gira (Antônio Jorge Souza dos Santos) wrote it and Daniela Mercury changed part of the lyric; the registered credit names both. A Rede Bahia interview quotes Tote Gira saying he wrote it in 1990 and Mercury recorded it in 1992. Year is the single year. The song is described as the recording that carried axé, then discussed as samba-reggae, across Brazil.

Funk carioca by MC Bob Rum (Moysés Osmar da Silva). The Portuguese song article says 1994. The English article and Bob Rum's biography tie the national success to the Som Livre compilation Rap Brasil Vol. 2 in 1995. Year 1995 is that compilation. The lyric uses the surname Silva for a favela resident. Letras.com also credits the writing to Bob Rum; that lyric page is not used as a source for the text.
